description: We are a team of four Computer Engineering students passionate about space, technology, and creativity. We aim to bring NASA’s forgotten space explorers back to life through an interactive storytelling experience combining technology and science. We are looking for creative, motivated teammates with skills in UI/UX, graphic design, 3D modeling, animation, storytelling, or web development. Above all, we value curiosity, teamwork, and sharing ideas !
summary: Echo Station is a free web app that turns a phone into a radio antenna for explorers aged 9 to 15. Belu, a young beluga who “sees” with echoes, has lost his friends: six real NASA robots that went silent across the solar system – Eagle on the Moon, Spirit, Opportunity and Ingenuity on Mars, Dawn around Ceres and Pioneer 10 heading out of the solar system. Players point their phone at the real sky; the signal grows when they aim at the true position of a robot, computed live from astronomy-engine and NASA JPL Horizons data (checked against Astropy: under 0.01° of difference). Each robot then tells its true story in seven short animated cards, with real NASA images and a mini-game that replays a real mission moment. The finale is Apollo 11’s laser mirror, which still sends echoes back to Earth. Echo Station shows young people that these machines are not forgotten: their discoveries still speak to us.
details:
WHAT ECHO STATION DOES

Echo Station is a free web app for explorers aged 9 to 15 (phone or computer, no install, no account). Belu, a young beluga who finds his way with echolocation, has lost his friends: six real NASA robots that went silent across the solar system – Eagle on the Moon, Spirit, Opportunity and Ingenuity on Mars, Dawn around Ceres, and Pioneer 10 heading out of the solar system. The phone becomes Belu's antenna: players point it at the real sky, and the signal grows when they aim at the true position of a robot. When they find it, the robot tells its true story, they play one of its real mission moments, and it becomes Belu's friend.

HOW IT WORKS – KEY TECHNICAL PIECES

1. Real sky positions. The Moon and Mars are computed live with astronomy-engine. Ceres and Pioneer 10 come from NASA JPL Horizons tables (DE441 ephemeris, one point per day from November 2026 to January 2028) that we generated and interpolate in the app. Everything is converted to azimuth and altitude for the player's location and time.

2. Proven accuracy. We compared our positions with Astropy: the difference is under 0.01° above the horizon (full table in docs/accuracy.md).

3. The phone antenna. We compute the direction of the back camera from the full 3-D phone rotation (W3C DeviceOrientation, rotation matrix R = Rz(alpha)·Rx(beta)·Ry(gamma)), so the aim stays stable even when the phone is tilted up toward the Moon. iPhones use the built-in compass heading. The direction is smoothed as a 3-D vector (no jump between 359° and 0°), and one tap on "Calibrate" while aiming at the Moon corrects the compass error. The app also handles the new motion-permission behaviour of recent Chrome versions.

4. Signal and lock-on. The signal level depends on the angle between where you aim and the target (20° tolerance). Holding within about 6° for 1.5 seconds locks on. A hysteresis rule stops the arrow from flipping between the Moon and Mars when they are close in the sky. Targets below the horizon stay findable: the arrow points down and "Belu hears it through the Earth".

5. Belu's sonar. Pressing "Click!" sends a sound: each friend answers with an echo whose delay grows with its distance from where you aim, coming from the left or the right (stereo) and higher-pitched when it is above you. A moving arrow guides players continuously; the click is optional.

6. A story for every robot. Each robot tells its story in seven animated cards: who I am, why I was sent, what I discovered (with a hands-on discovery moment), where I am now (a zoom from orbit onto the real landing site in LROC or HiRISE images, or the light-time distance for spacecraft in deep space), who took over (a timeline of later missions), friendship, and questions. The robot and Belu talk in speech bubbles with voices, sentence by sentence, and the sentence being spoken lights up in the text.

7. Five mission games that replay real moments: landing the Eagle past a boulder field with the real 1202/1201 alarms and limited fuel; driving Spirit backward with a stuck wheel to uncover silica (a sign of ancient hot water); keeping Opportunity alive through eight days of the 2018 dust storm; flying Ingenuity to photograph three spots for Perseverance and landing on airfield B despite gusts and drifting sand; and keeping a Deep Space Network dish on Pioneer 10's fading signal from 1972 to its last signal in 2003.

8. The finale. Players fire a laser at the mirror left on the Moon by Apollo 11 and see the real round trip of light (about 2.5 seconds), computed from the real Earth–Moon distance: like Belu, scientists still listen for echoes. When all six robots are found, Belu and his friends celebrate, and a "Start over" button lets the next player live the story from the beginning.

9. Scientist mode. For older players and teachers: live azimuth, altitude, RA/Dec, distance and light time for each target, with mission data and sources for every robot.

REAL NASA CONTENT

Every fact about the robots is sourced, mainly from NASA NSSDCA records, NASA and JPL mission pages, and LRO/LROC and MRO/HiRISE images, all listed in each robot's data file. The mission photographs keep their NASA credits.

ACCESSIBILITY AND DESIGN FOR 9–15

Audio guide for blind and low-vision players, written captions for every sound for deaf players, three text sizes, high contrast, a calm mode with no animations, vibration, keyboard controls, screen-reader labels, and a sky map that works without phone sensors. Short sentences, one task per screen, and no overstimulation.

RELIABILITY

A static web app hosted on GitHub Pages: no build step, no account, no tracking, and the location never leaves the device. Games load only when opened, and the app recovers if a file fails to download. We tested the full journey automatically on phone and desktop screen sizes (Playwright), plus 23 unit tests for the sky, guidance and data.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

The night sky becomes a classroom anyone can open with a phone. Young people connect real places in the sky to real missions and discover that "silent" hardware still teaches us: Moon rocks, signs of ancient water on Mars, salts on Ceres, the first powered flight on another planet. We want them to feel that exploration is a story they can join.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules), Canvas 2D, Web Audio, Web Speech, DeviceOrientation and Geolocation APIs, astronomy-engine, NASA JPL Horizons, Python and Astropy (accuracy check), Playwright and Node.js tests, GitHub Pages, Figma. Hardware: any smartphone with a compass and gyroscope, or a computer.

CREATIVITY

Echolocation links everything: belugas listen for echoes, radio antennas listen for spacecraft, and scientists still listen to laser echoes from the Moon. The robots are not "repaired": they become friends, and their discoveries keep speaking.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Honesty: Belu is fictional, every fact about the robots is real and sourced. Privacy: no account, no data collected. Accuracy: positions checked against Astropy. Inclusion: playable by blind, deaf and sensor-less players.

AI USE

Code was written with the help of Claude (Anthropic) and the robots' texts drafted with OpenAI Codex, then reviewed, tested and edited by the team. The six robot illustrations and the recorded robot voices are AI-generated: the images carry a visible "AI-GENERATED" watermark, and the voices are labelled on screen and in their file metadata. Belu was drawn by our team.

WHAT'S NEXT

French and Arabic versions, more silent robots (Viking, Sojourner, Phoenix, InSight), a camera view of the night sky, a classroom mode, sign-language videos, and an offline version for schools.

Source code and accuracy report: https://github.com/BouazizAicha/echo-station
